procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment of the Allahabad High Court dated October 25, 1956, which upheld the conviction under s. 295A of the Indian Penal Code but reduced the sentence.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The petitioner filed an appeal to the High Court at Allahabad. The learned Single Judge, by his judgment dated October 25, 1956, held that the article was published with the deliberate and malicious intention of outraging the religious feelings of muslims and that the petitioner was guilty under s. 295A of the Indian Penal Code. The learned Judge, however, reduced the sentence of imprisonment to 12 months and the fine from Rs. 2,000 to Rs. 250 only. An application for certificate to appeal to this Court under Arts. 132 and 134 having been rejected by the High Court on October 30, 1956
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The petitioner moved the Supreme Court for special leave to appeal from the judgment of the Allahabad High Court dated October 25, 1956. The petitioner also presented a petition under Art. 32 challenging the constitutional validity of s. 295A of the Indian Penal Code. The Supreme Court initially dismissed the stay application and the petition for special leave. The petition under Art. 32 has now come up for hearing.

directions: Set aside the judgment of the Rajasthan High Court.
Restore the judgment of the Sessions Judge.

issue.issue_text: Whether Section 295A of the Indian Penal Code is unconstitutional because it infringes the fundamental right to freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a) and is not a reasonable restriction in the interests of public order under Article 19(2).

law.name: Article 19(1)(a) of the Indian Constitution
law.description: Guarantees the fundamental right to freedom of speech and expression.

law.name: Article 19(2) of the Indian Constitution
law.description: Allows the state to impose reasonable restrictions on the right to freedom of speech and expression "in the interests of" public order, security of the State, decency, morality, etc.

law.name: Section 295A of the Indian Penal Code
law.description: Penalizes acts perpetrated with the deliberate and malicious intention of outraging the religious feelings of any class of citizens by insulting their religion or religious beliefs.

application.point: The Court first distinguished the scope of Article 19(2). It noted that the amended clause uses the phrase "in the interests of" public order, which is much wider than "for the maintenance of" public order. This means a law can be valid if it has a tendency to promote public order, even if it doesn't directly address an actual breach of it.
text_support: In the first place cl. (2) of Art. 19 protects a law imposing reasonable restrictions on the exercise of the right to freedom of speech and expression "in the interests of" public order. which is much wider than "for maintenance of" public order.

If, therefore, certain activities have a tendency to cause public disorder. a law penalising such activities as an offence cannot but be held to be a law imposing reasonable restriction "in the interests of public order" although in some cases those activities may not actually lead to a breach of public order.

application.point: The Court then analyzed the specific wording of Section 295A and found it to be narrowly tailored. It does not punish every insult to religion, but only the "aggravated form" of insult.
text_support: In the next place s. 295A does not penalise any and every act of insult to or attempt to insult the religion or the reiigious beliefs of a class of citizens but it penalises onlv those acts of insults to or those varieties of attempts to insult the religion or the religious beliefs of a class of citizens, which are perpetrated with the deliberate and malicious intention of outraging the religious feelings of that class.

application.point: The Court held that this requirement of a "deliberate and malicious intention" is key. Such an aggravated insult has a "calculated tendency" to disrupt public order. Therefore, the law targets speech that is inherently likely to cause public disorder.
text_support: It only punishes the aggravated form of insult to religion when it is perpetrated with the deliberate and malicious intention of outraging the religious feelings of that class.
The calculated tendency of this aggravated form of insult is clearly to disrupt the public order and the section, which penalises such acti\'ities, is well within the protection of cl. (2) of Arr. 19

application.point: Because the law is narrowly defined to only cover this specific, aggravated form of insult, the Court concluded that it could not be applied for purposes outside the constitutional limits. This distinguished it from previous cases where laws were struck down for being too broad.
text_support: Having regard to the ingredients of the offence created by the impugned section, there cannot, in our opinion, be any possibility of this law being applied for purposes not sanctioned by the Constitution.
In other words, the language employed in the section is not wide enough to cover restriction_ both within and without the limits of constitutionally permissible legislative action

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the challenge and upheld the constitutionality of Section 295A of the Indian Penal Code. It concluded that the section is a reasonable restriction on the freedom of speech and expression, permissible under Article 19(2) of the Constitution. The Court reasoned that the law is narrowly tailored to punish only the aggravated form of insult to religion—that which is done with a "deliberate and malicious intention"—which has a calculated tendency to disrupt public order, thus falling squarely within the phrase "in the interests of public order."

issue.issue_text: Whether Section 295A must be held to be wholly unconstitutional and void because its language is wide enough to cover restrictions both within and without the limits of constitutionally permissible legislative action.

facts: The petitioner argued that Section 295A of the Indian Penal Code is unconstitutional because its language is overly broad.

The argument was that the law could be used to punish acts of insulting religion that do not actually lead to public disorder, thereby covering actions both within and outside constitutionally permissible restrictions on free speech.
Because the law is not severable, the petitioner contended that the entire section must be declared void.
law: Article 19(2) of the Constitution allows for "reasonable restrictions" on the freedom of speech and expression "in the interests of" public order.
The court interprets the phrase "in the interests of" public order as being much wider than "for the maintenance of" public order.
A law that penalizes activities which have a *tendency* to cause public disorder is considered a reasonable restriction, even if a specific act does not actually lead to a breach of public order.
application: The Court first clarified that the constitutional test allows for restrictions on speech that has a mere tendency to cause public disorder, not just speech that actually causes it.
The Court then analyzed the specific wording of Section 295A and found that it is not overly broad. It does not penalize every insult to religion.
The section specifically targets only the "aggravated form of insult" which is perpetrated with the "deliberate and malicious intention of outraging the religious feelings" of a class of citizens.
The Court reasoned that this requirement of a deliberate and malicious intent narrows the scope of the law significantly. Insults made unwittingly or carelessly are not covered.
The Court concluded that this "aggravated form of insult," by its very nature, has a "calculated tendency... to disrupt the public order."

Therefore, the language of the section is not wide enough to cover actions outside the limits of constitutionally permissible restrictions, and there is no possibility of it being applied for purposes not sanctioned by the Constitution.
reasoning.conclusion: The Court rejected the argument, holding that Section 295A is not unconstitutionally broad. Its language, specifically the requirement of a "deliberate and malicious intention," narrowly targets only aggravated forms of insult that have a calculated tendency to disrupt public order, thus falling squarely within the reasonable restrictions permitted by Article 19(2) of the Constitution.

arguments.issue_text: Whether Section 295A of the Indian Penal Code is unconstitutional because it infringes the fundamental right to freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a) and is not a reasonable restriction in the interests of public order under Article 19(2).
appellant_arguments: Section 295A of the Indian Penal Code is ultra vires and void because it interferes with the petitioner's right to freedom of speech and expression guaranteed by Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution.
respondent_arguments: Section 295A is a valid law that falls within the protection of Article 19(2), which allows for reasonable restrictions on the freedom of speech in the interests of public order.

arguments.issue_text: Whether Section 295A must be held to be wholly unconstitutional and void because its language is wide enough to cover restrictions both within and without the limits of constitutionally permissible legislative action.
appellant_arguments: The language used in Section 295A is overly broad, covering restrictions on fundamental rights that are both within and outside the limits of what is constitutionally permissible.
respondent_arguments: The language of Section 295A is not overly broad and is well within the constitutionally permissible limits for restricting speech to protect public order.

cases.case_name: Debi Soron v. The State of Bihar
cases.principle: The expression 'in the interests of' in the amended Art. 19(2) makes the ambit of the protection very wide, meaning a law may not have been designed to directly maintain public order and yet it may have been enacted in the interests of public order.

cases.case_name: Om Prakash Gupta v. The State of U.P.
cases.principle: Section 403(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure and Article 20 of the Constitution (double jeopardy) have no application where there is only one trial for several offences, even if the accused is acquitted of some while being convicted of another.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A law that imposes restrictions on the freedom of speech and expression is constitutionally protected under the amended Article 19(2) if it is 'in the interests of public order'. This phrase is of wide ambit, and a law falls within its protection if the activities it penalizes have a tendency to cause public disorder, even if the law is not directly designed to maintain public order.
obiter: Under the original Article 19(2), a law restricting speech for 'public safety' or 'public order' was unconstitutional if it also covered activities that did not undermine the security of or tend to overthrow the State.
The contention that a law must be held wholly void if its language is wide enough to cover restrictions both within and without constitutionally permissible limits is not applicable in all cases.
'Public order' is an expression of wide connotation, signifying the state of tranquillity which prevails among the members of a political society.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: Section 295A of the Indian Penal Code is constitutionally valid as it does not penalize any and every act of insult to religion, but only the aggravated form of insult perpetrated with the deliberate and malicious intention of outraging the religious feelings of a class of citizens. This specific intent requirement narrows the law's application to acts that have a calculated tendency to disrupt public order, thus falling squarely within the ambit of reasonable restrictions permitted under Article 19(2) of the Constitution.
legal_tests_applied: The expression 'in the interests of' public order in the amended Article 19(2) is much wider than 'for maintenance of' public order. A law penalizing activities that have a tendency to cause public disorder is a law 'in the interests of public order', even if those activities may not actually lead to a breach of public order in some cases.

A law is not unconstitutionally overbroad if its language and the specific ingredients of the offense it creates are sufficiently narrow to prevent its application for purposes not sanctioned by the Constitution. The test is whether the law, by its own terms, is limited to constitutionally permissible restrictions.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant's reliance on the cases of Romesh Thappar and Brij Bushan was misplaced because those decisions were based on Article 19(2) as it stood before its amendment. The amended clause, which uses the wider phrase 'in the interests of... public order', makes the protection afforded to laws much broader.

The argument that the law is overbroad because insulting religion may not always lead to public disorder fails. The court found that Section 295A is not a general law against insulting religion; it specifically targets insults made with 'deliberate and malicious intention of outraging the religious feelings'. This aggravated form of insult has a 'calculated tendency... to disrupt the public order'.

The court rejected the contention that the law's language was wide enough to cover both permissible and impermissible restrictions. It held that due to the specific requirement of malicious intent, 'there cannot, in our opinion, be any possibility of this law being applied for purposes not sanctioned by the Constitution,' and therefore the question of severability does not arise.

The argument that offences relating to religion have no bearing on public order was deemed 'utterly untenable' by the court, which pointed to Articles 25 and 26 of the Constitution, where the right to freedom of religion is expressly made subject to public order.
why_respondent_won: The respondent's position was upheld because the court agreed that the amended Article 19(2) provides wide protection to laws enacted 'in the interests of' public order. The court found that a law penalizing activities with a 'tendency to cause public disorder' falls within this protection.

The court accepted that the language of Section 295A is not overly broad. It 'only punishes the aggravated form of insult to religion when it is perpetrated with the deliberate and malicious intention of outraging the religious feelings of that class.' This specific intent requirement sufficiently narrows the law to constitutionally permissible grounds.

The court found that the law is well within the protection of Article 19(2) as it imposes reasonable restrictions on speech, given that the 'calculated tendency of this aggravated form of insult is clearly to disrupt the public order.'
policy_considerations: The right to freedom of religion, as guaranteed by Articles 25 and 26, is explicitly made subject to public order, morality, and health. Therefore, it cannot be argued that freedom of religion has no bearing on the maintenance of public order, and laws creating offenses related to religion can be enacted in the interests of public order.
